props.title: Even Dwarfs Started Small
props.initialSlug: A chaotic revolt of dwarfs against authority

sections.content: Werner Herzog's bizarre and unsettling Even Dwarfs Started Small (1970) marks a radical departure in cinema's portrayal of rebellion and institutional chaos. Shot entirely with a cast of little people, the film creates an uncanny microcosm of society breaking down. It directly influenced later works like Gummo (1997) and The Holy Mountain (1973) in its raw, unflinching approach to societal outcasts. Herzog's decision to film in stark black and white on the volcanic landscapes of Lanzarote amplifies the apocalyptic atmosphere.

sections.content: The film's influence extends into modern experimental cinema, particularly in works that examine power dynamics and institutional rebellion. Titane (2021) and Border (2018) continue this tradition of using physical difference to challenge social norms. Herzog's unflinching camera work and documentary-like approach created a template for later filmmakers exploring marginalized communities. SUBHEAD: Breaking Cinematic Conventions

Herzog's techniques in Even Dwarfs Started Small deliberately subvert traditional film language. The chaotic scenes of rebellion, including the infamous crucified monkey sequence, inspired later provocateurs like Harmony Korine in Julien Donkey-Boy (1999) and Lars von Trier in The Idiots (1998). The film's rejection of traditional narrative structure paved the way for experimental works like Eraserhead (1977).
